With one appointment, you can also get protected against COVID-19, shingles, RSV, pneumococcal pneumonia and more. CVS® Pharmacy is here to help — all in one visit. Schedule vaccinations Learn more about your vaccine schedule The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends different routine vaccinations for different age groups. Explore the schedule information per age group below or visit the CDC immunization schedule page for more information on which vaccines are recommended. Last updated September 30, 2025, using U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) vaccine guidance. Vaccine Eligibility information Chikungunya Some travelers 12 years and older at higher risk of exposure to chikungunya virus or at increased risk of severe disease are recommended to receive an age-appropriate vaccine; those 60 years and older should not receive the live-attenuated vaccine at this time Cholera For people 2 to 64 years of age if traveling to an area where cholera is present or where the water and food are unsafe to drink Hepatitis A Any person who is not fully vaccinated and traveling to or working in countries with intermediate or high rates of hepatitis A Hepatitis B Eligible from 0 months* of age and older Japanese encephalitis Some people 2 months of age and older who are traveling to high-risk areas (e.g., Southeast and East Asia, the Indian subcontinent and parts of Oceania) Rabies Adults with high risk for exposure or post-exposure Tick-borne encephalitis ​(TBE) Ages 1 and older who are at increased risk for infection based on travel season, location, activities and duration Typhoid People 2 years of age and older who are traveling to high-risk areas where typhoid fever is of concern at least 2 weeks before travel Vaccines offered at CVS The CDC recommends the 2025/26 COVID-19 vaccine for: Adults 65 and older: Decision-making for vaccination is individually based.People 6 months* to 64 years at increased risk: Vaccination decisions are individually based and need-focused, emphasizing that vaccination is most beneficial for individuals who are at an increased risk for severe COVID-19 disease and less so for individuals who are not at an increased risk. The Centers of Disease Control and Prevention lists specific COVID-19 risk factors but also leaves the list open-ended, for people to consult with their medical provider or pharmacist regarding any other conditions or situations that can create a higher risk. Conditions that put you at higher risk, according to the CDC, include, but are not limited to: Being a past or current smokerBeing physically inactiveBlood disorders (including sickle cell disease)Body Mass Index greater than 25CancerChronic liver diseaseChronic lung disease, including cystic fibrosisDementia or a neurologic conditionDiabetesHeart disease, including high blood pressureHIV or tuberculosis infectionKidney diseaseMental health conditionsPregnancySolid organ or blood stem cell transplantSubstance use disordersWeakened immune systemAny other conditions or situations that place you at high risk of severe illness from COVID-19 (consult with your pharmacist or medical provider if you are unsure) *Subject to state law, COVID-19 vaccines for ages 5+ are available at select CVS Pharmacy® locations. COVID-19 vaccine for ages 18 months+ are available at all MinuteClinic® locations. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends an annual flu vaccination for nearly everyone 6 months of age or older, and our certified immunizers are able to vaccinate patients as young as 3 years old in some states. Get your flu shot to help reduce your risk of serious complications from the flu, including hospitalization. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends the hepatitis B vaccine for children and adolescents younger than 19 years of age, adults ages 19 through 59 who have not been vaccinated, adults ages 50 years and older with risk factors for hepatitis B infection, as well as infants. For infants born to hepatitis B negative mothers, the CDC recommends individual-based decision-making to decide whether to administer the hepatitis B vaccine at birth or begin the series later in infancy. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that the HPV vaccine be administered to individuals as young as 9 years old and those up to 26 years of age or if recommended by your health care provider. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that all 11 to 12 year olds get a MenACWY meningococcal vaccine with a booster dose at 16 years old. Those between 16 and 23 years old also may get a MenB meningococcal vaccine. The CDC also recommends a meningococcal vaccination for other children and adults who are at increased risk for meningococcal disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that children get two doses of MMR vaccine, starting with the first dose at 12 to 15 months of age, and then getting the second dose at some time between ages 4 and 6. Teens and adults should also be up-to-date on their MMR vaccination. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends an mpox vaccination for any person with known or suspected exposure to mpox and for specific populations that may be at higher risk of exposure to the mpox virus. Visit the CDC web page on mpox to learn more about the vaccine. Call your local CVS® for vaccine availability. Schedule vaccinations The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends this vaccine for: Adults 50 years of age or olderPatients 19 through 49 years of age or older who have certain medical conditions or risk factors To help protect children from the effects of a polio infection, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that children get four doses of polio vaccine, each at the following stages: 2 months of age, 4 months, 6 through 18 months, then at ages 4 through 6 years. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that the following adults get one lifetime dose of the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine to provide protection against serious RSV illness: People 75 years or olderPeople between 50 and 74 years old and at increased risk of severe RSV (have certain chronic health conditions or live in a nursing home) Women who are 32 through 36 weeks pregnant during September through January are recommended by the CDC to get one dose of maternal RSV vaccine to help protect their babies. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends two doses for two groups: Adults ages 50 and olderAdults ages 19 and older if they have a weakened immune system from disease or therapy The Tdap vaccine can help prevent tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis (whooping cough). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that all adolescents receive their first Tdap vaccine, and it highly recommends that they receive it before they become teens, getting that first shot at age 11 or 12. After that dose, they should continue to receive a Tdap vaccine for booster immunization at least once every 10 years. A different vaccine, DTaP, is used with infants and children for these conditions. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends two doses of chickenpox vaccine for children, adolescents and adults. Children should receive two doses of the vaccine — the first dose between 12 and 15 months old and then the second dose between ages 4 and 6 years old. Call your local CVS® for vaccine availability. Schedule vaccinations Travel vaccines Chikungunya virus is spread to people by the bite of an infected mosquito. Outbreaks have occurred in Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and islands in the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Chikungunya vaccine is recommended for some travelers at higher risk of exposure to chikungunya virus or at increased risk of severe disease. Schedule vaccinations Visit a doctor or travel clinic to talk about cholera vaccination if you're going to an area where cholera is present, or where the water and food are unsafe to drink and eat. Schedule vaccinations The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends a hepatitis A vaccination for unvaccinated children and teens through 18 years of age and adults at higher risk for getting a hepatitis A infection, as well as those 19 years of age and older who are not at higher risk and seek protection. Hepatitis A virus is contagious and spreads through close person-to-person contact and eating contaminated food or drink. Call your local CVS® for vaccine availability. Schedule vaccinations The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends the hepatitis B vaccine for children and adolescents younger than 19 years of age, adults ages 19 through 59 who have not been vaccinated, adults ages 50 years and older with risk factors for hepatitis B infection, as well as infants. For infants born to hepatitis B negative mothers, the CDC recommends individual-based decision-making to decide whether to administer the hepatitis B vaccine at birth or begin the series later in infancy. You should consider this vaccination if you plan on spending time in a country where this infection is regularly reported. The risk of infection is higher for travelers going to places such as Southeast Asia, India and Oceania, especially if traveling for longer periods of time or during the transmission season, if spending time in rural areas or doing outdoor activities, or staying in accommodations without air conditioning, screens or bed nets. Schedule vaccinations Rabies is a fatal but preventable viral disease. Patients should consider the human rabies vaccine preventively if they work directly with animals that could have rabies, or if they travel to parts of the world where rabies is common and access to medical care is limited. Talk to your health care provider about whether the human rabies shot is right for you, for prevention or after possible exposure. Schedule vaccinations TBE virus is mainly spread through the bite of an infected tick. This virus can be found in parts of the region stretching from western and northern Europe to northern and eastern Asia. The TBE vaccine is a three dose vaccine series approved for patients ages 1 year and older. A booster dose may also be given in certain patients with prolonged exposure. Schedule vaccinations If you plan on traveling to an area where typhoid infections are a concern, this vaccination can help protect you from getting typhoid fever. Typhoid is contracted when someone eats or drinks contaminated food or drink. The bacteria can multiply and spread into the bloodstream, causing typhoid fever. Typhoid fever is common in many regions of the world, including parts of East and Southeast Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and Central and South America. Immigration-related vaccines We have vaccines that may be needed When applying for a green card or adjusting immigration status, there are vaccines required by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to complete Form I-693. A civil surgeon is required to complete this form. CVS can share vaccine documentation* and offers vaccines, such as chickenpox (varicella), hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningitis (meningococcal), MMR, pneumonia (pneumococcal), polio and Tdap at eligible locations. Age and other restrictions apply.* What you should know about why to get vaccines How vaccines help protect your health Vaccines help strengthen your body’s natural defenses* against specific viruses and bacteria, making them the safest, most effective way to help protect you and your family from the risks associated with related illness and hospitalization.* The CDC recommends reviewing your immunization history at every health care visit. Updated vaccines may be needed for work, travel or school. View your vaccination records Vaccine basics A preparation that is used to stimulate the body’s immune response against diseases. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Explaining how vaccines work. CDC.gov. Published August 10, 2024. Vaccines help your body protect itself from diseases. When you get vaccinated, your body activates a natural defense. The vaccine imitates a virus or bacteria. Your body reacts to this imitation by producing antibodies. This is called an immune response. The antibodies your body makes after a vaccine can recognize specific germs. Your antibodies know how to fight these familiar germs if they return. After antibodies are activated from a vaccine, you might notice mild side effects. These side effects may last a day or two. Some people get a headache or body aches. However, these side effects don't mean you have an infection. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Explaining how vaccines work. CDC.gov. Published August 10, 2024. Vaccines are important for global health. Here are some benefits of vaccination according to the World Health Organization: Vaccines help save millions of lives every year.Vaccines help your body fight diseases by helping to train the body on how to defend against certain infections.Vaccines help stop diseases from spreading across communities.Vaccines help reduce serious complications from infections.Vaccines are safe and effective for many people. Most children and adults can safely get vaccinated. World Health Organization. Vaccines and immunization . WHO.int. Published January 27, 2025. Active immunity results when someone is exposed to a disease-causing organism that triggers the immune system to produce antibodies to that disease. Passive immunity is provided when someone is given antibodies to a disease. A vaccination refers to the process of receiving a vaccine whereas an immunization refers to the process by which a person becomes protected against a disease through vaccination. Insurance coverage for vaccines Many insurance plans will cover some or all costs of select vaccinations. To ensure coverage, contact your insurance provider. Medicare Part B covers preventative care vaccines for flu, COVID-19 and pneumococcal pneumonia at no cost. Medicare Part B also covers hepatitis B vaccines for certain patients at no cost. Medicare Part D covers preventative care vaccines for shingles, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis or whooping cough) at no cost. Certain other vaccines, such as vaccines used for treatment purposes or vaccines not recommended by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), may be covered with cost sharing. Visit Medicare.gov to learn more. Getting vaccinated Getting several vaccines during the same visit is called coadministration. Most vaccines work well when given together, as well as when administered separately. Coadministration can make vaccination quick and convenient. Most vaccines can be administered on the same day, but some cannot. Your health care provider can help determine which vaccines can be given together. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Multiple vaccines at once. CDC.gov. Published December 20, 2024. There are some people who should not get certain vaccines* or should wait to get them due to age, specific health conditions or other factors. It’s always a good idea to discuss with your health care provider the vaccinations you are considering. According to research completed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC’s) Public Health Law Program (PHLP) in 2019, DTaP, MMR, polio and varicella vaccines are required for children entering school in almost every state, and the meningitis (meningococcal) vaccine is required for entry into later grades in many states. To find out what vaccines are required for your individual situation, please contact your local school district or specific college. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. State school immunization requirements and vaccine exemption laws . CDC.gov. Accessed January 15, 2025. Consult with your doctor or other health care provider to determine which vaccines during pregnancy are recommended for you and your baby, depending on your age, lifestyle, medical conditions and other factors. Some recommended vaccines during pregnancy include: Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis, which is also known as whooping cough)FluRespiratory syncytial virus (RSV) The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has guidance on the specific timing for when each vaccine is the most useful for protecting you and your baby. Yes, trained MinuteClinic providers can administer 15 vaccinations, including meningitis (meningococcal), Tdap for adults, DTaP for youths, flu, tetanus and COVID-19. Vaccine safety Vaccines go through years of testing and are continuously monitored for safety and efficacy once licensed and in use. U.S. teams of physicians, scientists and public health experts closely monitor any adverse effects that might occur after a vaccination and respond as necessary to ensure vaccines are held to the highest safety standards. You may experience mild side effects after receiving a vaccine. Most side effects are mild (for example, a sore arm or low-grade fever) and go away within a few days. More information on each vaccination is available on the specific vaccine health pages. https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/basics/possible-side-effects.html Unvaccinated people can be at risk if exposed to vaccine-preventable diseases. Symptoms and complications of such diseases can be serious and even life-threatening.
